notes.meaning: Josiah became king when he was only eight years old, after his ungodly father Amon was killed. He ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years, and the text names his mother, Jedidah. Pious guardians likely helped raise him and taught him to love God. Early training in godliness can shape a person's life for good.

Josiah lived a life that pleased God, following the good pattern of his forefather David. He kept strictly to God's path without turning off to the right hand or to the left. He did not become overly strict on one side or careless on the other, but walked with steady obedience. Wholehearted devotion means following God's commands without straying.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, King Josiah sent his royal secretary, Shaphan, to the house of the Lord. By this time, Josiah had already begun seeking God and clearing out idols, but now he turned his attention to the building itself. He was ready to organize a major repair of the temple.

Josiah told Shaphan to instruct Hilkiah the high priest to count the silver that the people had given at the temple entrance. The gatekeepers had collected these voluntary gifts over time to help maintain the building. Josiah wanted these funds totaled up so the repair work could be paid for.

The king ordered the money to be handed over to the supervisors in charge of the temple repairs. They were to use the funds to pay carpenters, builders, and stonecutters, and to buy wood and cut stone to fix the crumbling building. The house of the Lord had been neglected for generations, and it was time to rebuild it.

The officials did not demand receipts or records from the foremen because the men were known to be completely honest. They managed the funds with deep integrity and faithfulness to God. When God's people do their work with true honesty, they earn the trust of everyone around them.

While the temple was being cleaned and repaired, Hilkiah told Shaphan that he had found the Book of the Law. This sacred scroll had been lost or hidden during the reigns of wicked kings who hated God's word. Shaphan took the book and began reading it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars argue that this book was not an ancient Mosaic scroll, but a newly composed version of Deuteronomy produced to justify Josiah's religious centralization.

notes.meaning: Shaphan returned to King Josiah and reported that the temple funds had been emptied and given to the builders and supervisors. He gave a faithful accounting of his first task before mentioning anything else. The repairs to God's house were moving forward smoothly as ordered.

Shaphan then told the king that Hilkiah the priest had given him a book, and he read from it in Josiah's presence. He read key portions of the scroll, including the blessings for obedience and the curses for rebellion. Hearing God's written word brought the truth directly to the king's ears.

When Josiah heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes in deep grief and terror. Tearing one's clothes was an outward sign of profound sorrow and horror over sin. He realized how far the nation had drifted from God and how dangerous their situation was.

Josiah immediately sent a group of his highest leaders to act on what had been read. The group included Hilkiah the high priest, Shaphan the royal secretary, and other trusted royal officials. Josiah treated God's message with urgent respect by sending the most important men in the realm.

Josiah commanded the men to seek the Lord's counsel for him and for all Judah concerning the book that had been found. He knew that God's holy anger burned against them because their ancestors had neglected these commands. When we see our sin clearly in Scripture, our first response should be to turn to God for mercy.

The delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, who lived in the newer section of Jerusalem and was married to Shallum, the keeper of the wardrobe. Huldah was well known for speaking the true word of God, and she was close at hand in the capital while other prophets were away. The officials laid the king's urgent question before her.

differ.view: Huldah was a true prophetess delivering God's inspired word, but her private message to the king's messengers did not establish an ongoing governing office over men in the church.
Huldah's role in instructing the high priest and top royal officials shows that God calls and authorizes women to exercise high-level spiritual leadership and teaching.

notes.meaning: Huldah began by declaring the words of the Lord, telling the messengers to take a reply back to the man who sent them. She spoke with prophetic boldness rather than court manners, putting the earthly king on the same level as any other human being before God. God's truth applies equally to all people, no matter how powerful they are.

The Lord declared that He was going to bring terrible ruin on Jerusalem and its inhabitants. This destruction would match every warning and curse written in the book the king had heard. God is completely faithful to His word, both in giving blessings and in carrying out judgments.

God explained that judgment had to come because the people had forsaken Him and burned incense to handmade idols. Their persistent rebellion had provoked His righteous anger. His wrath was now like a blazing fire that would not be put out.

Huldah then gave a separate, personal word from God for King Josiah himself. Even though national judgment was settled, God noticed how Josiah had responded to the reading of the law. God sees the heart of each individual, even when a whole society is corrupt.

God noted that Josiah's heart was tender, meaning he was sensitive to God and quick to repent, which means turning from sin back to the Lord. The king had humbled himself, torn his clothes, and wept before God when he heard the warnings of ruin. Because Josiah was brokenhearted over sin, God promised that He had heard his prayers.

The Lord promised Josiah that he would die and be buried before the terrible ruin fell upon Jerusalem. Although he would later die of wounds from a battle, he died at peace with God and was spared the sight of his city being crushed and carried into exile. The messengers carried this comforting message back to the king.
